title: A spectator at the ground: where to stand, how to photograph and support
summary: A safe place, silence while shooting, hearing protection, photos without flash and the right kind of support: what a spectator needs to know.

body.html: Spectators are welcome at many shooting grounds, but people are shooting nearby, so spectators follow safety rules too. Stand only where it is allowed: in the spectator area, usually behind the stand or behind a fence or rope. Do not step in front of the firing line (the line the shooters stand on) or walk where targets fly, even if nobody seems to be shooting.
If you are not sure where to stand, ask the referee or the organiser. If you bring children or a dog, keep them close, and follow the ground staff’s instructions: they are there for your safety.

Everyone near a layout (the shooting area with its stands and traps) needs hearing protection, not only the shooters. The rules of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting both name spectators. In Sporting™, children outside the clubhouse wear it at all times.
If you stand close to a stand, wear safety glasses too; in Sporting™ the rules require them for anyone close to a stand. Small target fragments sometimes fall from above, so a cap also helps.
Do not touch guns, cartridges or equipment. Keep away from the traps (the machines that throw the clays): they can go off unexpectedly and hit hard.

While a shooter is on the stand, keep quiet: no loud talk, clapping or shouting, and put your phone on silent. Applaud when the shooter has finished the stand or the round and nobody on the layout is about to call for a target.

Photos and videos are a lovely way to keep memories, but safety matters more than the picture. Shoot only from the spectator area, and do not step forward for a better angle. Do not use flash, which can dazzle the shooter, and turn off the shutter sound.
Do not move in the shooter’s line of sight while they are aiming. A drone needs the organiser’s permission, and the drone rules of the country always apply.
Respect privacy. Before you post photos of people, especially children, ask for their consent or their parents’. Some competitions have the organiser’s own rules on filming, so check them in advance.

How can you support your shooter? Do not give advice during the competition: the rules treat it as coaching. The shooter can get a yellow card, and the referee sends the adviser out of the shooting area. Do not comment on the referee’s decisions either. In Compak® Sporting the rules count open criticism of a decision by a spectator as an attempt to influence the referee. In Sporting™ that rule names the other shooters, but spectators are expected to keep quiet too: the referee keeps order on the stand.

Good support is calm. Bring water, help carry things, smile after the round and talk about the score later, once emotions have settled. A calm spectator makes the day easier for the shooter and the whole squad.

key_points.html: Stand only in the spectator area, not in front of the firing line
Hearing protection for spectators too; glasses if you stand close
Quiet during shooting; applause when the shooter has finished
Photos from the spectator area, with no flash and no shutter sound
No advice during the competition and no criticism of the referee

did_you_know.html: Many striking clay shooting photos are taken from the side and slightly behind the shooter, inside the spectator area: they show both the gun and the breaking target.

quiz.q: Does a spectator need hearing protection?

options.text: No, only the people who are shooting
Yes, the rules require it near the layout
Only at championships, not at club shoots

quiz.explain: Both rulebooks require hearing protection for shooters, referees, staff and spectators near the layout.

quiz.q: May you take photos with flash?

options.text: Yes, if you stay in the spectator area
Only once the referee has agreed
No, because flash can dazzle the shooter

quiz.explain: Flash distracts and dazzles the shooter, so spectators do not use it.

quiz.q: What happens if a spectator coaches a shooter during a competition?

options.text: The shooter can get a yellow card; the adviser is sent away
Nothing at all, as long as the advice is given quietly
The shooter must shoot the whole stand again from the start

quiz.explain: Advice during a competition counts as coaching, which both rulebooks forbid.
